slides.title: A fast-growing market nobody has made pay
Demand is real: US quick-commerce grocery sales nearly tripled in three years, to $5.1B in 2025

claims.claim: Demand is real: US quick-commerce grocery sales nearly tripled in three years, to $5.1B in 2025
evidence: 2.8x 2025 sales as a multiple of 2022

claims.claim: The founders are right about the market
evidence: Every year: growth ran between 38% and 44%, in line with the founders' 'over 40% a year'

claims.claim: 2025: the largest yearly gain in dollars, so the market is not slowing down
But sales are not profit: the operators behind this growth still lose money

slides.title: Neither incumbent makes money on the orders it delivers, whatever its scale

claims.claim: Both lose a quarter or more of revenue at the EBITDA line
evidence: EBITDA margin 2025: Zipcart (national) -25.8%; QuickBasket (regional) -45.7%
Zipcart −$310M on $1,200M, QuickBasket −$96M on $210M

claims.claim: Each order loses money, more so at the smaller operator
evidence: Contribution per order 2025: Zipcart -$1.9; QuickBasket -$3.4

claims.claim: QuickBasket, the regional model closest to Parcelbird Now, closed 4 of its 11 cities in 2025

slides.title: Zipcart's only profitable city got there by charging customers more, at the cost of 14% of its orders

claims.claim: Losing money on each order nationally
evidence: Zipcart lost $1.90 on each order in 2025 across its network
Its densest city was the best case for rider routes and store volume
The founders cite this city as proof that 'it can be done'

claims.claim: The fix was pricing, not operations
evidence: Added a new $3.99 service fee on every order
Cut promotions to 1% of order value
Kept the same stores and riders; density was already the highest in its network

claims.claim: Impact
evidence: $0.4 contribution per order in that city, Q4 2025
−14% change in order volume in that city after the fee

claims.claim: Parcelbird's plan does not use this lever: it keeps the $1.99 fee and relies on bigger baskets instead

slides.title: Unit economics of Parcelbird Now
At the benchmark median each order loses $2.67 before store costs, with rider time as the biggest drain

claims.claim: At the benchmark median each order loses $2.67 before store costs
evidence: Per order: Margin on goods 9.18; Promotions -2.04; Delivery fee 1.99; Picking and packing -3.1; Rider time -7.4; Payment and packaging -1.3; Contribution per order -2.67

claims.claim: Rider time eats most of the margin on goods
evidence: 80.6% of the margin on goods goes to paying riders
Rider time: $17.75 an hour spread over 2.4 deliveries; two of the three cities are weighing minimum pay rules

claims.claim: Pay rules: each $1 an hour on rider pay costs about $0.42 per order at this productivity
After store costs: rent, staff and utilities add $3.50 per order at 900 orders a day, taking the loss to $6.17

slides.title: The founders' plan rests on inputs no site has reached, least of all Parcelbird's own Columbus test

claims.claim: The founders' plan rests on inputs no site has reached
evidence: Average order value: Columbus $31; median $34; best $42; plan $45 — Plan is $3 above the best site
Promotions: 12%; 6%; 6%; 2% — Plan assumes a third of the median
Orders per rider-hour: 2.1; 2.4; 3; 3.5 — Plan is above the 1.9–3.0 range
Orders per store per day: 280; 900; 1,400; 1,800 — Plan is above the 400–1,400 range
Contribution per order: −$6.2; −$2.7; $0.5; $3.8 — Clearly positive only in the plan / The best-site column mixes two sites; no site achieved both

slides.title: Rider speed and basket size, both beyond the best site observed, carry most of the plan's profit

claims.claim: Two operating bets do most of the work
evidence: Contribution added per order: Rider speed 2.32; Basket size 2.31; Promotions 1.8
72% of the $6.44 gap between plan and median comes from rider speed and basket size

claims.claim: Rider speed: 3.5 deliveries an hour sits above the top of the 1.9–3.0 benchmark range
Basket size: a $45 basket is $3 above the best site and $14 above the Columbus pop-up
Promotions: the plan's 2% is a third of the median, while the pop-up needed 12% to grow

slides.title: Only Zipcart-style fees make a median order pay — and even then the store needs above-median volume

claims.claim: Bigger basket needed to break even is above the best site and the plan's $45
evidence: Needed $46.7; median $34; best $42; Columbus $31

claims.claim: Faster riders needed are above the top of the 1.9–3.0 range
evidence: Needed 3.8; median 2.4; best 3; Columbus 2.1

claims.claim: Zipcart fees: works per order, unproven per store
evidence: Needed 1,043 orders per store per day; median 900; best 1,400; Columbus 280
Earns $3.02 an order, but needs 16% more volume than the median after losing 14% to the fee
$3.99 fee on top of the $1.99 delivery fee, promotions at 1%; the store covers its $1.15M fixed cost

slides.title: Demand is softer in practice than in the survey: only 22% of pop-up customers still ordered in month three

claims.claim: Demand is softer in practice than in the survey
evidence: Said they would use it at least weekly 44%; Still ordering in month three 22%
Survey n = 1,500 Columbus residents aged 25–39; the two groups differ

claims.claim: Each lasting customer is expensive to win
evidence: $173 of acquisition spend per customer still ordering in month three ($38 ÷ 22%)

claims.claim: Pop-up growth: orders rose 18% a week, but on promotions of 12% of the basket
Filling a store: 900 orders a day takes about 8,830 regular customers at 3.1 orders a month, or about $1.53M of acquisition
At median margins: each lasting customer loses about $8.28 a month, so that spend is never earned back

slides.title: Cash and the runway rule
Even on the founders' numbers, the plan leaves $2.5M at month 18, half of a year's runway at today's burn

claims.claim: The plan leaves $2.5M at month 18
evidence: Cash today $12M; Parcelbird Now to month 18 $9.5M; Cash at month 18 $2.5M
The $9.5M: capex of $5.4M for nine stores, launch marketing and operating losses, all on the plan's own unit economics

claims.claim: No buffer if the plan slips
evidence: The floor: 12 months at today's burn needs $4.8M; the plan leaves $2.3M less
Runway left at month 18: 6.2 ($2.5M ÷ $0.4M burn a month)

claims.claim: Acquisition: the plan's density at pop-up retention would cost about 2.9 times the whole $9.5M
evidence: Acquisition to fill nine stores at 1,800 orders a day: $27.5M
17,661 regular customers × $173 × 9 stores

slides.title: Each dark store would lose about $2.0M a year at median economics, the network more than Parcelbird's cash

claims.claim: Each dark store would lose about $2.0M a year at median economics
evidence: 328,500 orders a year per store × −$2.7 contribution per order − $1,150,000 fixed cost = −$2.03M result per store a year, before acquisition and head office

claims.claim: The estimate is generous to the plan
evidence: The store reaches the median of 900 orders a day; the Columbus pop-up averaged 280
Customer acquisition and launch marketing are not counted

claims.claim: Nine stores at this level would lose about $18.27M a year, 1.52 times Parcelbird's $12.0M of cash
Rider pay rules in two of the three cities would add about $0.42 per order for each $1 an hour

slides.title: The software-led alternative
The software pipeline could add up to $3.6M of ARR, close to doubling the business, for $0.8M a year of hires

claims.claim: Deals already near signing
evidence: $0.9M ARR from the 9 late-stage grocers at $96,000 a year each
About 21% of today's $4.1M ARR
About $0.70M of gross profit a year at the 81% margin

claims.claim: Pipeline could add up to $3.6M of ARR
evidence: $3.5M ARR if all 37 pipeline grocers sign
87% of today's ARR
Several want fast delivery from their own stores, which the software already runs
Parcelbird Now would turn these buyers into competitors in its three cities

claims.claim: The only new spend the software plan needs
evidence: $0.8M a year for 2 engineers and 2 sales hires
Full-pipeline gross profit would be 3.6 times this cost
Hiring can follow signed contracts, unlike $5.4M of store capex

slides.title: The software can break even in 2029 within current cash if growth holds beyond today's pipeline

claims.claim: The software can break even in 2029 within current cash
evidence: Breakeven ARR $11.0M
$8.9M costs a year ÷ 81% gross margin = $11M
Cash used before breakeven, 2027–28: $6.6M ($8.92M a year of costs less gross profit on ARR growing 60% a year)

claims.claim: Affordable, but it depends on new sales
evidence: 72 new contracts needed to reach breakeven (($11.0M − $4.1M) ÷ $96,000)
Pipeline: 72 contracts is about twice the 37 grocers in today's pipeline

claims.claim: At 40% growth: breakeven slips to 2030 and cash falls to about $2.61M, still a year of runway at the lower burn

slides.title: Of the three options, only the software-led plan keeps a year of runway and a credible route to profit

claims.claim: Founders' plan: Reject
evidence: $9.5M extra cash
No: $2.5M left at month 18
Only on inputs beyond the best site
About $2.0M a year lost per store at the median

evidence: About $2.43M in year one
Only just: about $4.77M left after a year
Loses about $0.30M a year even at median volume
Competes with the grocers Parcelbird sells to
$0.6M capex + $0.30M store loss + $1.53M acquisition = $2.43M

claims.claim: Software-led: Recommended / Fund the hires now and pace them to contract wins
evidence: Yes: about $6.62M used before breakeven
Breakeven in 2029 at 60% growth
Needs about 72 new contracts

assumptions_and_uncertainties: Synthetic benchmark data; every figure from the board briefing pack
If the stores still lose money at month 18, or the $9.5M excludes the software business's own burn, cash runs out sooner
The best-site column mixes two sites; no site achieved both
Survey respondents and pop-up customers: the two groups differ
Two of the three cities are weighing minimum pay rules; each $1 an hour on rider pay costs about $0.42 per order
Not every deal will close (pipeline values at the $96,000 average contract)
Software breakeven depends on new sales: about 72 new contracts, about twice today's 37-grocer pipeline
At 40% growth: breakeven slips to 2030 and cash falls to about $2.61M
Annual model: revenue = average of opening and closing ARR; costs held at today's level plus the hires
Per-store estimate is generous to the plan: assumes median 900 orders a day; acquisition and launch marketing not counted
next_steps: Decline Parcelbird Now for 2027 and set the reopen test: a customer site covering its store costs with higher fees — Board, January 2027
Hire the 2 engineers and 2 sales staff, released in step with late-stage contract signings — CEO, Q1 2027
Package fast delivery from existing stores for the pipeline grocers that want it — Product lead, H1 2027
Report ARR, monthly burn and runway against the 12-month floor at every board meeting — Finance lead, From Q1 2027
